name: photos
title: Sort your photos into folders by year and month
pitch: Thousands of photos in one folder? Your program will read the date each photo was taken and put it in a 2024/05 folder. You start by making one folder, and end with a tool you can trust with your memories.

steps.do: Create a test folder by hand and COPY some of your photos into it. Copy them: your program could destroy them.
steps.done: a test folder holds copies of a few photos.
steps.hint: Take photos from a phone and from a camera if you can: they don't all store their date the same way.
steps.why: Photos can't be downloaded again. Working on copies until you trust your program is not optional here.

steps.do: Create your .py program and make it create a folder for this year.
steps.done: a folder named after this year (like 2026) appears.
steps.hint: Look at `os.makedirs` or `pathlib.Path.mkdir`, and `datetime.date.today().year` for the year.
steps.why: Your first program that changes the disk. Start with the smallest action you can check by eye.

steps.do: Run your program a second time: it crashes because the folder already exists. Fix that.
steps.done: you can run it twice in a row without an error.
steps.hint: Both `os.makedirs` and `Path.mkdir` have an option for "it's fine if it's already there".
steps.why: Real programs run again and again. A program that only works the first time is a trap: making it safe to re-run is a habit worth learning now.

steps.do: Inside the year folder, create a folder for the month.
steps.hint: Paths can be built piece by piece: `Path("2026") / "10"`. Think about "10" versus "1" for October and January.
steps.why: Writing months with two digits (01, 02… 12) keeps them sorted in the right order everywhere, even in a file manager that sorts names as text.

steps.do: Write a function `make_folder(year, month)` that creates the year/month folder for any date.
steps.done: calling it with any year and month creates the right folder.
steps.hint: Move the code you already have into a `def`, and replace the fixed values with parameters.
steps.why: A function gives a name to a piece of work, so you can use it again without copying it. This is the moment your script starts to have a structure.

steps.do: Now we need to read the photos: open a photo file from your program.
steps.done: your program opens one photo and closes it without an error.
steps.hint: `open(path, "rb")`, inside a `with` block. A photo is binary data, so the "b" matters.
steps.why: Every file is just bytes. Text files are bytes your program reads as letters; a photo is bytes in a format a library knows how to read.

steps.do: Reading photo dates needs a library: create a virtual environment and install Pillow with pip.
steps.done: `from PIL import Image` works in your program.
steps.hint: `python3 -m venv`, activate it, then `pip install Pillow` (the package is Pillow, the module is PIL).
steps.why: Nobody writes everything from scratch. Knowing how to add a library to one project, without touching the rest of your system, is part of every real project.

steps.do: Look up what EXIF is, and read a photo's EXIF data to find the date it was taken.
steps.done: your program prints the date of one photo.
steps.hint: Pillow's `Image.open(...).getexif()` gives a dictionary-like object. The date tag is called DateTimeOriginal (it can also sit in DateTime).
steps.why: EXIF is information the camera writes inside the photo: date, camera model, sometimes the place. Reading it means your program knows what the file name doesn't say.

steps.do: Write a function that turns the EXIF date into the year and month your `make_folder` function needs.
steps.done: it returns (2024, 5) for a photo taken in May 2024.
steps.hint: The EXIF date looks like "2024:05:17 14:03:22". `datetime.strptime` can read it, or you can split the text.
steps.why: Turning data from one format into another is a large part of programming. Doing it in its own small function makes it easy to test with a few examples.

steps.do: Handle photos with no EXIF date: use the file's modification date, or put them in an `unknown` folder.
steps.done: a screenshot (it has no EXIF) gets sorted too.
steps.hint: `Path.stat().st_mtime` gives the modification time, and `datetime.fromtimestamp` turns it into a date.
steps.why: Real data is messy: screenshots, edited images, photos from messaging apps often lose their EXIF. A tool that only handles the perfect case breaks on the first real folder.

steps.do: Dry run: for every photo in the folder, print where it would go (`IMG_001.jpg -> 2024/05`) without moving anything.
steps.done: the list looks right for all your test photos.
steps.hint: Loop over the files, call your functions, and only `print` for now.
steps.why: Real tools have a dry-run mode because checking a plan is cheap and undoing a mistake is not. Use it every time a program is about to move many files.

steps.do: Copy the photos into their folders. Move them only once you trust your program.
steps.done: every photo is in its year/month folder.
steps.hint: `shutil.copy2` copies a file and keeps its dates; `shutil.move` moves it.
steps.why: Copy first, delete later: if something went wrong, nothing is lost. `copy2` keeps the original dates, so the copies stay as faithful as the photos.

steps.do: Handle two photos with the same name in the same month: don't let one overwrite the other.
steps.done: two IMG_0001.jpg from the same month both survive.
steps.hint: Before copying, check if the target exists; if it does, add a number to the name (IMG_0001_2.jpg).
steps.why: Cameras reuse names (IMG_0001 comes back after 9999, and two phones count the same way). Silently overwriting a file is one of the worst bugs a program can have, because nobody notices until it's too late.

steps.do: Optional: group year and month into an object (a class or a dataclass) and use it in your functions.
steps.done: the program still sorts everything the same way.
steps.hint: Look at `@dataclass` from the dataclasses module: a few lines give you a small class with fields.
steps.why: Changing the inside of a program without changing what it does is called refactoring. Having a dry run and test photos is what makes it safe.
